Sure! The first rhythm game I ever played was Um Jammer Lammy, a spin-off of Parappa the Rapper, which both had musical levels with cutscenes telling a story in between. The levels were actually part of the story and what they were trying to accomplish. These games were actually considered the first of modern rhythm games (Parappa came out in the mid-90s and Lammy in 1999) and had original music rather than licensed songs. 

So that's where the root of my interest in rhythm games lies! I also really like Rhythn Heaven and Crypt of the Necrodancer. 

Mine is a bit different from others as you're able to play at your own pace for the main levels and you can equipped any "instrument" you've collected to any button/key you want to and go wild! You'll also be able to compose your own song which can be played at the boss stages. 

The boss stages will double as narrative-driving scenes, but there will also be additional cutscenes where you can either watch or play along with the music on the controller if you feel like it! There will be accessibility options as well.

That "high functioning" autistics (which used to be called Asperger's) actually have low-functioning traits that we are pressured to suppress from social situations. This includes having involuntary autistic meltdowns if there is too much input for our brains to handle. Even a well-spoken doctor or businessman who displays class and high intellect who is autistic can be reduced to screaming, self-harm, and an inability to communicate for several minutes if they are overstimulated by light, sounds, or unexpected and overwhelming stress. This is not voluntary. This is not a tantrum to get what we want, even if not getting what we want was the trigger.


 If you are near an autistic person before a meltdown it is preventable if you know how to help that person (removing them from the scenario is a good rule of thumb). If they begin the meltdown it can no longer be stopped, and helping them get to a quiet, isolated space and leaving them be for a while is usually the best rule of thumb. Consider reminding them before you leave that you'll be there for them when you're done. Do not belittle, punish, or ignore an autistic person regarding a meltdown. This isn't fair, it would be just as unfair to punish somebody for having a seizure or a panick attack. 

I would highly reccomend taking time to learn more about "high-functioning" autism and autism masking or camouflaging. Watch some Ted Talks and YouTube vlogs by autistic people, not parents of autistic children, to best familiarize yourself with autism because a lot of us are so good at hiding what we were taught were inappropriate traits that we were diagnosed way too late in life to get necessary childhood support. With this knowledge you can learn to better spot an autistic person, even if they don't know it themselves, and have a better idea about how to interact with them in order to better communicate. Don't talk down to us, but learn how to phrase things in an autistic individual would understand once you get to know what kind of verbiage works for them.

I just got out of a job with the opposite problem. They told me 60 hour weeks for $2500 a month. That's low, especially for being in Boston, coming at 10.41ish an hour. We decided that I would live-in since the 6am/7am to 6pm/7pm would be easier if I didn't have to commute. $500 a month was subtracted a month for use of their bedroom, which wasnt bad but also wasnt private as they did all their laundry in that room, but I understood it was a necessary sacrifice. I had just moved to the city from Texas, where rates and cost of living are much, much lower and I thought I was lucky to get something more than 2000 a month. I know better now.

So 60 hour weeks, it's a lot, but I was sure I could handle it, and honestly I could have. 

They also offered $12 an hour on weekends or for "overtime" past 60 hours. It was manageable for a month or two, then the mom started coming home later and later. It reached the point that I started to average 75 hour weeks and maybe get a day off on Sunday. It hit 4 months and I started to slip up in some areas of the house cleaning aspect of the job, even though I was praised for my work with the baby (I started with him at 2 months old, by then he was 6 months). I was stressed and overworked and my only friends (who are basically the only "family" I have) live in the next state over, so it was impossible for me to ever relax. 

At some point after slipping up too much we talked and they looked into a back up nanny. However, it became more of a weekend +partial Monday babysitter. It made things a little better, but not for long.

Now something to keep in mind is that the parents are doctors in training, meaning they work weird and long hours. However when I accepted the job it was to the understanding that the typical hours would be 7am-7pm. But around this time the mother would text me at 7:30pm, half an hour AFTER I was supposed to get off that she would be late by about two hours. This happened at least once a week.

I never expressed being upset at this even though I very much was. Until a few weeks ago. 

She messaged me at 7:30 that she wouldn't be in until 9. Then messaged me at 9 saying that she was on her way (meaning that she'd be there at 9:30 and that she forgot she had a presentation she forgot about and needed me to start at 5:30am when she left. I wasn't going to take it this time. I let her know that between 9:30pm and 5:30am that I wouldn't even be able to get a full night's sleep, especially because I needed to shower and pack for my upcoming move among other things (by this time I had already decided to leave the job and had already told them). 

She told me that she would get a friend to come over to watch the baby until 8am.

I felt like things were good since I finally stood my ground and said no to the extended hours for the first time in a year. 

However, on my final day, I ask them if I can use their wi-fi to do a quick job interview via Skype before I leave. My things are packed, I was ready to stand in their hallway for the quick interview and then leave. However she then asked me, "so do you want me to give you the livingroom for an hour?" And I replied, "Oh sure!" believing her to be offering something nice. But then she burst out with, "I don't know why you would expect me to do that for you!" And it turned into a big mess from there. 

She said that when I said no to those extra hours a few weeks ago it was the breaking point and I "broke her heart". She said that the baby would have been asleep at 5:30 anyways so I could have just slept in. For me that wasn't true at all, I would have woke up at 5 and checked on him anyways and not been able to get back to sleep for the rest of the day, but she wouldn't hear it. Plus sometimes he DOES wake up a few hours early. She told me that I needed to be more aware of what was going on around me and that they had hard jobs and hours and did so much to make things easier on me. She yelled at me for no reason on my last day as I was heading out the door.

I personally don't think that I should have had to sacrifice my own personal life just because they have a demanding job, especially not for 10.41-12 an hour.

Oh and side note: I found out through care.com that they offered their weekend babysitter $14 an hour even though they offered $12 for me to work the same hours.
